blocks.h2: What Does an Ejector Pump Do?
blocks.body: An ejector pump sits in a sealed basin in the basement floor. Wastewater from fixtures below the sewer line, like a basement toilet, shower, laundry or bar sink, drains into the basin. When it fills, the pump lifts the water up and out to the main sewer line. In homes with an [overhead sewer system](/arlington-heights/overhead-sewer-systems), every basement drain flows to the ejector pit, so the pump is what keeps your basement from backing up.

img.alt: J. Blanton plumber working on the discharge pipe of a basement sump pump

blocks.h2: Signs Your Ejector Pump Is Failing
blocks.intro: Stop using basement fixtures and call if:

tiles.h3: The High-Water Alarm Is Going Off
tiles.body: The basin is filling and the pump isn't keeping up.
A sealed basin shouldn't smell. A broken seal or vent problem lets gas out.
Upstairs is fine and downstairs isn't. The pump or check valve has failed.
A stuck float, a failed check valve or a worn motor.

blocks.h2: Ejector Pumps in Arlington Heights Homes
blocks.intro: Ejector pumps are common here, for two reasons.

items.body: Many older homes added an overhead sewer after storm backups like the one in July 2011. In those homes, the ejector pump handles the whole basement, so a failure is urgent.

items.h3: Newer Homes Built With Overhead Sewers
items.body: Homes built here since the late 1970s or early 1980s were required to have overhead sewers. Their original ejector pumps may now be on their second or third replacement.
A bathroom added to a 1950s or 1960s basement almost always drains to an ejector basin. Those installs vary a lot in quality, and we see plenty of undersized pumps.

blocks.h2: What Happens When You Call J. Blanton
blocks.intro: An ejector failure is a sewage problem, so we treat it like one.

steps.body: Stop using basement fixtures and call. Our line is open 24/7.
A stuck float or bad check valve is a repair. A burned-out motor means a new pump, sized to your fixtures.
You get a flat-rate price before we open the basin.

blocks.h2: Ejector Pump Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: What's the difference between an ejector pump and a sump pump?
items.preview: A sump pump moves groundwater. An ejector pump moves sewage.
items.answer: A sump pump sits in an open pit and pumps clean groundwater outside. An ejector pump sits in a sealed basin and lifts wastewater from basement fixtures up to the sewer line. They're built differently and aren't interchangeable.

items.q: What should I do if the ejector alarm goes off?
items.preview: Stop using basement fixtures, keep the lid sealed and call.
items.answer: Stop using everything that drains to the basin, including the washer, and leave the lid sealed. Then call us, any time.

items.q: How long does an ejector pump last?
items.preview: Often 7 to 10 years or more, depending on use.
items.answer: Many last somewhere between 7 and 10 years or more. Wipes, grease and heavy use shorten that. If yours is original to a 1990s home, it's worth having it checked.

items.q: What can't go down a basement toilet with an ejector pump?
items.preview: Wipes, paper towels, grease and anything but toilet paper.
items.answer: Only toilet paper. Wipes, even the flushable kind, paper towels and grease clog the pump and wear it out early.

items.q: I just had an overhead sewer installed. What maintenance does the ejector need?
items.preview: A yearly check of the pump, float and check valve.
items.answer: Have the pump, float and check valve checked once a year, and test the alarm. Keep wipes and grease out of every drain that feeds the basin.

items.q: How much does ejector pump replacement cost in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: It depends on the pump, basin and access. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on the pump, the basin, the check valve and venting and how easy it is to reach. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
